readerTitle: Twice the ads, barely more customers
caseNote: 가상 사례 (가정 청소 업체, 소규모 사무실 대상 IT 지원 회사) + 4P 개념의 출처 (McCarthy 1960, Booms & Bitner 1981) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 4P는 네 개의 부서 업무가 아니라 한 제안을 네 방향에서 본 것이다. 광고는 나머지 세 P가 만든 결과를 키울 뿐이어서, 막힌 곳이 다른 P에 있으면 광고를 늘릴수록 고객 한 명당 비용이 오른다.
misconception: 손님이 안 늘면 광고를 더 하거나 가격을 내리면 된다. 마케팅은 곧 홍보다.

sources.text: McCarthy, E. J. (1960). Basic Marketing: A Managerial Approach. Irwin.
Borden, N. H. (1964). The Concept of the Marketing Mix. Journal of Advertising Research.
Booms, B. H. & Bitner, M. J. (1981). Marketing Strategies and Organization Structures for Service Firms. In Marketing of Services, American Marketing Association.
청소 업체와 IT 지원 회사의 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 분해 계산: 문의 120 − 영업시간 외 전화 48 = 연결 72, 72 − 토요일 희망 30 = 견적 42, 예약 18 (18 ÷ 42 = 43%). 예약하지 않은 사람 120 − 18 = 102명 중 가격을 듣기 전에 빠진 사람 48 + 30 = 78명(76%, 'more than three in four').
4P를 1960년 McCarthy가 정리·대중화했다는 점, 'marketing mix'라는 용어는 Neil Borden이 먼저 쓴 것으로 알려져 있다는 점을 게시 전 확인하세요. 카드에는 McCarthy가 'popularized'했다고만 적었습니다.
서비스업 확장 7P(People, Process, Physical evidence)의 출처를 Booms & Bitner(1981)로 적었습니다. 서지 정보를 다시 확인하세요.

cards.title: Twice the ads, barely more customers
body: A home-cleaning company spends $1,000 a month on local ads and gets 15 new bookings. That's about $67 per new customer.
The owner doubles the budget to $2,000. Inquiries double too, from 60 to 120. Bookings go from 15 to just 18. Each new customer now costs **$111**.

image.label: A ringing phone next to a closed office sign
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 저녁 시간, 'Closed' 팻말이 걸린 작은 청소 업체 사무실 문 앞에서 전화기가 울리고 있음. 창밖으로 광고 전단이 잔뜩 붙은 동네 게시판. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The ads doubled inquiries. Most didn't book.
body: The extra $1,000 clearly brought people in. But 102 of the 120 people who got in touch never became customers.
Where should you spend your next hour?

options.text: Rewrite the ads so they sell harder
options.feedback: The ads already did their job by doubling inquiries. Stronger copy would bring even more people to the same leak.

options.text: Cut the price 15% to win over more inquiries
options.feedback: You'd give up margin on every booking without knowing price was the problem. If it wasn't, you paid for nothing.

options.text: Trace what happened to the 102 people who didn't book
options.feedback: The loss happened after the ad. Finding exactly where tells you which lever to pull, and it costs only time.

cards.title: Where 120 inquiries went.
body: More than three in four lost inquiries never even heard a price. They were lost to *when* and *how* people could buy.

breakdown.label: Booked
breakdown.detail: 43% of those who got a quote

cards.title: The 4Ps
body: The **4Ps** are the four things every business decides when it brings an offer to customers. Marketing professor E. Jerome McCarthy popularized the list in 1960.
list: **Product:** what you sell, including hours, options and service
**Price:** what customers pay, and on what terms
**Place:** where and how they can buy
cards.callout: The owner pushed Promotion. The leaks were in Place and Product.
cards.softwareNote: In software, Place is the choice between self-serve sign-up, an app store or a sales team. A great ad can't fix a sign-up page that asks for a credit card before users see any value.

cards.title: Promotion multiplies the other three.
body: The Ps aren't four separate jobs. They're one offer seen from four sides, and customers judge the whole thing at once.

When the offer fits, more promotion brings more customers. When one P is broken, more promotion brings more people to the break. That's the twist here: doubling the ads made each customer about **67% more expensive**.
An online booking form and a few Saturday slots might have done more than the second $1,000.

image.label: Four connected dials labeled Product, Price, Place, Promotion
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 하나의 기계에 다이얼 네 개(Product, Price, Place, Promotion)가 달려 있음. Promotion 다이얼은 최대로 돌아가 있지만 Place 쪽 파이프에 구멍이 나서 물(고객)이 새고 있음.

cards.title: It's a seller's checklist, not a customer insight.
body: The 4Ps list what you control. They don't tell you who you're serving or what that person wants. Decide that first, then set the four levers to match.

For services, some marketers add People, Process and Physical evidence, because staff and the visit itself are part of what's sold. And the levers pull on each other: Saturday slots may mean higher wages, which touches Price.

cards.title: Now it's an IT support firm.
body: You provide IT support to small law offices. Your sales team books plenty of meetings, and prospects say the service sounds great. Few sign.
Your only plan is a 24-month contract at $1,800 a month, sold in person. Which lever do you pull first?

options.text: Spend more on ads to book more meetings
options.feedback: Meetings aren't the problem. More of them would raise your cost per signed client without fixing why prospects stall.

options.text: Offer a three-month starter plan before the long contract
options.feedback: A two-year commitment is a big risk for a small office. A short starter plan changes the terms and the product without cutting your monthly price.
It might help, but it costs you on every client. If the real worry is being locked in for two years, a lower price won't remove it.

cards.title: Find the broken P before you push the loud one.
body: Product, price, place and promotion are one offer. Promotion only multiplies what the other three already do.
**Try it today:** follow your last ten lost customers. Write down where each one dropped off, then label it Product, Price, Place or Promotion.
